opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd be a little careful with the framing first. I can't speak to the exact details of any internal policy, and these things often sound more dramatic in headlines than they are in practice. But the broader trend is real, and I think it's worth unpacking.

The core idea is that much of the most valuable knowledge in a company isn't written down anywhere. It lives in people's heads: how a senior engineer debugs a weird production issue, how a researcher decides which experiment is worth running, how someone weighs trade-offs in a design review. Historically, that knowledge transferred slowly through mentorship, code review, and osmosis. What's changing is that companies now see a path to capturing those decision traces directly and turning them into training signal for models. That's "distillation" in the broad sense. You're not just distilling a big model into a small one; you're distilling human expertise into a system.

Why now? I think three things are converging. First, the public data that powered the first wave of large models is largely exhausted. The next gains come from high-quality, process-level data: not just the final answer, but the reasoning and actions that led to it. Second, agents are becoming capable enough that this kind of data is directly useful. If you want a model to work like an engineer, you need examples of how engineers actually work, step by step. Third, there's intense competitive pressure. Every major lab is looking for a data advantage, and your own employees are a proprietary source that nobody else has.

There's an uncomfortable side to this, and I don't want to gloss over it. When people are asked to teach a system to do what they do, they naturally wonder whether they're training their replacement. I think that's a legitimate concern, and companies need to be honest about it rather than wrapping it in nice language. In my view, the more realistic near-term outcome is that routine parts of the job get automated, and the bar for what counts as valuable human contribution moves up: having taste, setting direction, asking the right questions, noticing when the system is confidently wrong.

There's also a technical subtlety. Distilling human behavior captures what people do, not necessarily why, and not necessarily what's optimal. If you imitate experts, you also imitate their blind spots. So I suspect the real long-term value isn't pure imitation. It's using human traces as a starting point, then letting models improve through search, verification, and reinforcement, the way AlphaGo started from human games and then went beyond them.

So I see this less as a one-off corporate policy and more as a signal: we're moving from an era where models learn from the internet to one where they learn from work itself. That's a big shift, and how companies handle the human side of it will matter a lot, both for trust and for whether the knowledge they capture is any good.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from learning from internet data to learning from work, and says human traces should be supplemented with search and reinforcement. It does not argue that surviving this trend requires moving beyond the existing paradigm.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I can only speak from my own perspective, not for Meta's internal decisions. But if you step back, the trend itself is not surprising at all, and it's not really a Meta-specific story.

Think about what has happened in the last couple of years. Training a frontier model from scratch is enormously expensive, both in compute and in the sheer amount of human effort it takes to get the data right. At the same time, we've learned that once you have a strong model, a huge fraction of its capability can be transferred into smaller or more specialized models at a tiny fraction of that cost. So from a pure economics point of view, distillation has moved from being a nice-to-have trick to being the main production pipeline. The big model becomes something like a teacher, or maybe a factory, and most of what actually gets deployed is a student.

Once you accept that, the organizational consequence follows naturally. If the leverage is in distillation, then the people who understand the product, the domain, the evaluation, all need to be part of that process. You can't have a small research group produce a giant model and then throw it over the wall. The question of what to distill, for whom, and how to measure whether the student is actually good is deeply tied to the people who own each use case. So asking everyone to participate is, in a sense, admitting that the hard problem has shifted from "can we train it" to "can we shape it for a thousand different purposes."

There's a second layer that I find more interesting as a researcher. Distillation is a kind of knowledge compression, and we still don't fully understand what gets lost. A student model can match a teacher on a benchmark and still miss the reasoning structure underneath. If you involve a lot of people and a lot of different tasks, you start to see those failure modes much faster. In that sense, broad participation is also a way of collecting signal about where the compression breaks. That's valuable scientifically, not just operationally.

And then there's the competitive dimension, which I think everyone can see. The industry is converging on the view that model weights alone are not the moat. What matters is how quickly you can turn a capable base into something useful in a specific context, and how much tacit knowledge inside the company flows into the model. Requiring employees to engage with distillation is one way of turning that institutional knowledge into training signal. Whether that is the best way, I honestly don't know. It depends a lot on how it's done, whether people feel it's meaningful work or just a chore.

So my short answer would be: the broader trend is that the center of gravity in AI is moving from pretraining to post-training and transfer, and organizations are restructuring around that. The specific policy is one expression of a much larger shift, and I'd expect to see versions of it everywhere, not just at one company.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from pretraining toward distillation, post-training, and transfer, but does not argue that surviving this trend requires moving beyond the existing paradigm.

astra-6.text:
I think the broader trend is that companies want to turn individual expertise into organizational capability. An employee knows how to approach a problem, which tools to use, and how to judge whether a result is good. A lot of that knowledge is implicit. Asking employees to participate in distillation is, in effect, asking them to make that knowledge available for training AI systems.

Here, “distillation” can mean something broader than having a smaller model imitate a larger model. The teacher can also be a person, or a person working with AI. The valuable information isn’t just the final answer; it’s the process: what you tried, where you made a correction, and why you accepted one result over another.

I wouldn’t infer Meta’s exact implementation or intentions from that requirement alone. But the direction is interesting: employees increasingly contribute both by doing their jobs and by helping improve the systems that do parts of those jobs. That creates a real tension. It can make everyone more productive, but employees may also wonder how sharing their expertise changes their own role. Whether this works well depends on the incentives, the quality of the feedback, and how the company handles that uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response describes employees turning expertise into AI training data and broadens the meaning of distillation, but it does not argue that surviving this trend requires moving beyond the existing paradigm.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look at it as part of a broader shift: AI development is becoming less about training one giant model and more about turning that model’s capabilities into something useful, efficient, and widely deployable.

Distillation is one way to do that. You use a stronger model to provide examples or guidance for a smaller model, so the smaller one can handle particular tasks at lower cost and latency. But the difficult part isn’t simply generating a lot of answers. It’s deciding which tasks matter, what a good answer looks like, and how to tell whether the student model actually learned the capability. That’s where employees’ domain knowledge can become valuable.

Without knowing the details of Meta’s requirement, I’d interpret the broader trend as bringing more people into that process. Researchers build the underlying capabilities, while people across the organization help define tasks, identify failures, and evaluate results. In that sense, employees are increasingly contributing to the development of AI, rather than only using it.

The important question is whether that participation produces a useful learning signal. If everyone is just submitting examples to meet a quota, the value could be limited. If their expertise helps create better tasks and more reliable evaluations, it can make a real difference.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward making models efficient and involving employees in development, but it does not argue that surviving this trend requires moving beyond the existing paradigm.
